summary: Describes ingress filtering mechanisms and their generic issues, with particular attention to the effects on multihomed networks. BCP 38, RFC 2827, limits the impact of DDoS attacks by denying traffic with spoofed addresses. This best current practice updates RFC 2827.

eli5.summary: A guard at a school gate checks that arriving kids really come from the school they claim. This explains how that check works when a network has more than one gate.

questions: how to filter spoofed addresses with multiple isps
subtitle: How routers can drop packets with forged source addresses without breaking networks that connect to more than one ISP.

tldr.problem: BCP 38 (RFC 2827) asks ISPs to drop traffic whose source address a customer has no right to use, but a simple filter can wrongly discard legitimate traffic from multihomed or asymmetrically routed networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes five ways to implement ingress filtering (access lists, Strict RPF, Feasible RPF, Loose RPF, and Loose RPF ignoring default routes) and three approaches for multihomed sites to live with them.
tldr.outcome: Strict RPF or Feasible RPF can almost always be used between an ISP and an edge network, while plain Loose RPF is not recommended except to spot unrouted addresses. The RFC updates RFC 2827 and is itself updated by RFC 8704.

today: RFC 3704 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2827, and it has itself been updated by RFC 8704. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Ingress Filtering Exists
sections.content:
RFC 3704 builds on RFC 2827 (BCP 38), which recommends that ISPs drop traffic entering their networks from a source address the customer network does not legitimately use. The filtering covers, but is not limited to, so-called Martian addresses: reserved ranges such as 10.0.0.0/8, 127.0.0.0/8 and 192.168.0.0/16.

The reasoning is that distributed denial of service attacks often spoof source addresses. Sometimes the address is a random number inside the target network, which makes machines there attack others. Sometimes it is a random 32-bit number, so the real source is hard to trace. Filtering at the edge suppresses such traffic early and lets attacks be traced back to at least their source networks.

The document is aimed at ISP and edge network operators who want to learn about ingress filtering, or who already use it and want to avoid the pitfalls in multihomed and asymmetric setups.
sections.eli5: Some bad guys write a fake return address on their mail. If the post office checks every letter leaves from the address it claims, fake addresses get caught early.

sections.title: Five Ways to Filter
sections.content:
The RFC lists at least five ways to implement RFC 2827. An Ingress Access List checks the source address of every packet on an interface against a list of acceptable prefixes and drops anything that does not match. It is the most deterministic approach, but it is usually maintained by hand, so an outdated list can block legitimate traffic, for example after a customer adds prefixes by multihoming.

Strict Reverse Path Forwarding (Strict RPF) is conceptually the same but dynamic. The router looks up the source address in its Forwarding Information Base (FIB), and the packet passes only if it arrived on the interface that would be used to reach that source. It is simple, cheap, fast and dynamic, but it only works where routing is symmetrical, and it filters legitimate traffic if a legitimate prefix is not advertised or not accepted.

Feasible Path RPF extends Strict RPF by also adding alternative paths (all, or N of the feasible BGP paths) to the table used for the check. It relies on consistent route advertisements reaching every router that does the checking; as a general guideline, if an advertisement is filtered, the packets are filtered too.
sections.eli5: One guard reads from a written list of allowed families. Another asks the map, "would I send a reply back through this same gate?" A third accepts any gate that leads back to the same family.

sections.title: The Loose RPF Variants
sections.content:
Loose RPF only checks that a route to the source exists, even a default route, and not where it points. The RFC calls it a "route presence check" and notes it is a misnomer because there is no reverse path check at all. Packets from Martian or unrouted addresses are dropped, but because it gives up directionality it cannot limit an edge network to traffic it legitimately originates, which in most cases makes it useless as an ingress filter.

Default routes make this worse: ISPs use them for things like honey pot systems or for transit from a larger provider, and where the check does not look at where the default route points, a default route nullifies Loose RPF completely. Loose RPF ignoring default routes excludes default routes from the lookup, so it is mostly usable where default routes are only there to catch bogus sources and explicit routes cover the legitimate traffic. It also loses directionality.

Both variants fit places with asymmetric routing, such as inter-ISP links, and an ISP filtering its upstreams to get rid of Martian addresses. They can also serve as contract verification, showing that another network did at least some ingress filtering, but they cannot detect an address taken from someone else's address space.
sections.eli5: The loose guard only asks, "Is this a real address anywhere?" A made-up address gets stopped, but a real address that belongs to someone else walks right through.

sections.title: Where to Apply Filtering
sections.content:
Ingress filtering is not only for the last-mile link between an ISP and a customer. The RFC says it is fine and recommended to filter at ISP edges and at routers connecting LANs to an enterprise network, which adds defense in depth. Because the issue is recursive, any special arrangement a user negotiates with an ISP should also hold on the ISP's upstream and peering links, so manual models that do not propagate information to every party have only limited usefulness.

Filtering also protects your own infrastructure. Unless every border blocks the use of your own addresses as source addresses, attackers may bypass the access restrictions that protect routers and other equipment. On peering links, a mechanism such as Strict RPF works well as long as routing between the peers stays reasonably symmetric, and different links may have different contracts, trust and technical options.
sections.eli5: Checking at every door, not just the front one, keeps the whole building safer, including your own bedroom.

sections.title: Multihoming Solutions
sections.content:
A site may multihome to back up its connectivity, to use whichever ISP is offering the fastest TCP service at the moment, to reach places where no single ISP serves, or while changing ISPs. The RFC lists six options: do not multihome, do not filter, accept incomplete service, weaken filtering with a loose RPF check, make each ISP's filter complete, or send traffic only to the ISP whose prefix it uses. The first three are listed for completeness and are not viable positions.

Loose RPF cannot be recommended, except as a way to measure whether Martian or other unrouted addresses are being used. Making each ISP's filter complete usually means the edge network has provider-independent prefixes and exchanges routes with its ISPs over BGP, so it must be big and capable enough to qualify for its own address assignment and an autonomous system number. Feasible RPF and Strict RPF with operational techniques both work well here. Where customer data comes from databases such as Radius, TACACS or Diameter instead of a routing protocol, Strict RPF or access lists can be generated automatically from them.

The third approach suits smaller edge networks with provider-based addressing: route traffic sourced from a provider's address space only to that provider. This takes careful planning. An edge network may connect to each ISP through two or more Points of Presence, or use tunnels, and if an exit router is chosen for every prefix, traffic from any other prefix can simply be discarded.
sections.eli5: If a family uses two gates, either tell both guards about the whole family, or make everyone leave by the gate that matches their note.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Advice
sections.content:
The closer to the real source filtering is done, the more effective it is: a first-hop router can check a neighboring host exactly, while a router further away can only confirm that such a system could exist in the prefix. So filtering should happen at several levels. It is also impossible to know whether a given attacker is behind a filter, so source addresses can only be guessed to be spoofed, but a lead is still valuable.

The RFC summarizes the trade-offs. Access lists are the most bulletproof when done properly but need manual upkeep. Strict RPF is an easy and sure choice between an edge network and its ISP. Feasible RPF suits the same cases and multihomed ones, but assumes routing information is originated and propagated consistently. Loose RPF mainly filters unrouted prefixes.

Its conclusions: always filter between an ISP and a single-homed edge network; Feasible RPF or similar Strict RPF techniques can almost always be used for multihomed edge networks; both ISPs and edge networks should check that their own addresses are not arriving as sources from outside; and some filtering between ISPs is reasonable, especially when the number of prefixes is low.
sections.eli5: The closer the guard stands to the kid, the better the check. And it is worth checking at many places, not one.

A route to the source exists, even a default route
